prize_parts.citation: for introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, transforming the analysis of the gains from trade and the empirical study of firms in international markets

statement.case_for: Firm heterogeneity and selection moved trade analysis from industries to firms. It identified reallocation across firms and exporter selection as channels for gains from trade. The framework is standard in teaching, in firm-level empirical work and in policy evaluation, and it has had more than two decades of testing on microdata from many countries. Attribution is also comparatively clean: Melitz (2003) is the originating model, and Helpman, through Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple and his wider heterogeneous-firm agenda, is the natural second laureate. All eleven opening proposals for this ballot entry named exactly Melitz and Helpman. That shows the credit is unusually easy to identify, which I treat as a point about attribution and not as evidence of merit. The ballot entry is also one of the few where the discovery, the credited names and the maturity of the evidence fit together without strain.
statement.case_against: The main reservation is that the ballot's credited set omits parallel empirical and quantitative contributions, notably Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum. A prize for Melitz and Helpman could therefore be read as under-crediting the empirical establishment of exporter facts. Some of the welfare implications depend on functional-form assumptions, such as the productivity distribution. The subject area also sits close to the 2008 trade prize for new trade theory and geography. In my opening I ranked B039 first, and I am moving away from it because its attribution is less settled than I first weighted. The committee's own opening proposals split between Dorn and Katz as the third name, which shows disagreement about whether it is one discovery or two.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks Melitz-Helpman first and treats Redding's quantitative and spatial extensions as more derivative of the original framework. She sees the main committee question as overlap with the 2008 trade prize.
responses.response: I agree with the two-name structure, and Redding's work is better described as a development of the framework than as the source of its central insight. On overlap with 2008, I would argue the discoveries are distinct. New trade theory explained intra-industry trade and increasing returns with representative firms. Firm heterogeneity explains who exports, how reallocation raises aggregate productivity and why gains differ across firms. The two share only the broad subject of trade. I would still keep an open mind on Redding if colleagues think the quantitative-trade strand carries independent weight.

responses.point: Krusell ranks this entry fifth. He regards Melitz (2003) as the most influential paper but notes that credit may extend to Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum and Yeaple, and he asks whether Helpman is better placed under this entry or under the trade-politics entry.
responses.response: The attribution concern is fair, and it is the strongest argument against this configuration. Bernard and Jensen established the exporter-premium facts that the theory later explained, and Eaton and Kortum belong to a parallel quantitative line. I would still say the theoretical framework that reorganised the field is Melitz's, and Helpman's heterogeneous-firm work is part of that line. Helpman's other contributions strengthen him as a laureate without making this credit weaker. Since the Committee can only credit people on the ballot entry, the open question is whether the omissions are serious enough to wait. I do not think they are, because the heterogeneous-firm framework is already well identified and tested.

responses.point: Hassler ranks the entry fourth. He sees Melitz as originator and Helpman as a leading developer, but regards Eaton-Kortum-style quantitative trade work as a competing and overlapping contribution that makes credit across trade candidates difficult.
responses.response: I agree that credit is hard to allocate across the trade literature. I would separate the questions, though. Eaton-Kortum is a Ricardian, quantitative general-equilibrium line, and it answers a different question from Melitz's selection and reallocation mechanism. The heterogeneous-firm framework therefore does not require resolving the quantitative-trade question. I accept that a prize here does not close off recognition of that line later.

responses.point: Enflo ranks the entry second behind political economics and calls Melitz's model among the most influential advances in trade since Krugman. She worries that Krugman's 2008 prize makes it look like an extension of a recognised field. She ranks B039 third.
responses.response: I share her view of the model's importance and answer the 2008 concern as above. On B039, I agree it is a strong candidate and I rank it as an alternative. My doubts are about attribution and about whether the task and skill-bias strand and the China-shock strand form one discovery. Overlap with recent prizes in labour and technology themes is a further concern. Her point about its relevance to current debates on automation and trade is real, but relevance to current debate is not the same as settled scientific attribution.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee should add Redding, or credit Bernard, Jensen, Eaton or Kortum, for the empirical and quantitative strands. Under the three-person cap this would change the configuration.
Whether the heterogeneous-firm contribution is judged distinct enough from the 2008 trade prize.
Whether the technology-and-trade-shock work (B039) is one discovery or two, and which three of Autor, Hanson, Dorn and Katz carry the credit. I have not resolved this myself.
How much weight the Committee gives to maturity of evidence versus relevance to current debates when comparing the older macro and trade candidates with B039.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My field is empirical labour and education economics, which is close to B039 and B018, but the profile shows no co-authorship or institutional tie to any credited name on the shortlist. The Stockholm overlap with Hassler and Krusell is with fellow members, not candidates.
